subtype: Stage 3: The target's confusion and shame [Receiver]
passage:
Monday
My stomach hurt again this morning, right when I was tying my shoes. It always hurts on school days, never on Sundays. Mummy gave me ajwain water and said I eat too fast.
In class Tejas called me Sumit Snotty again and everyone laughed. Maybe it's because I'm slow at kabaddi. Maybe if I was funnier they would stop. I think it's my fault somehow.
Urmila didi asked why her little brother looks so sad these days. I said "nothing, tests." If I tell Mummy, she will go to school and shout, and then Tejas will know I told, and it will be worse.
So I just won't say anything.
Sumit

qa.a: It hurts on school days, never on Sundays, like this morning while he was tying his shoes.

qa.q: Why does Sumit think it is his own fault?
qa.a: He is confused and ashamed, so he guesses the teasing happens because he is slow at kabaddi or not funny enough.

qa.q: What could help Sumit break the secret at this stage?
qa.a: Urmila didi could gently keep asking and tell him it is not his fault, then help him tell their mother calmly, so an adult can deal with it safely without him being blamed for telling.

qa.q: What might Urmila didi be noticing from her side?
qa.a: She sees her brother looking sad for days and hears "nothing, tests," which may not sound like the whole truth to her.

grounding: It shows a boy who gets stomach aches before school, blames himself for the teasing and hides it from his family for fear of making it worse.

passage: Every morning at the bus stop outside Sirsa, Pawan held his stomach. "Again?" his mother Vandana asked, tying his tiffin. "Just a little," he said. On the bus, the older boys flicked his ears and called him "chuha." He sat by the window and counted poles so he wouldn't cry. At school he wondered what was wrong with him. Maybe his ears really were too big. Maybe he should laugh along. That evening, when Vandana asked how his day was, Pawan said, "Good." He thought about the time Papa went to the sarpanch over a small fight and the whole village talked for weeks. No. If he told, everything would get bigger. He pulled the blanket up and stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did the older boys call Pawan on the bus?
How can you tell Pawan feels ashamed?
qa.a: He wonders what is wrong with him and whether his ears are too big, and he tells his mother his day was "Good" instead of the truth.

qa.q: What turning point could Vandana offer at this stage?
qa.a: Since the stomach aches come every school morning, she could sit with Pawan calmly, ask about the bus and school, and promise to handle it quietly with his teacher, so he feels safe telling.

qa.q: What is Vandana probably experiencing right now?
qa.a: She sees her son holding his stomach daily and may be worried and puzzled, not knowing that fear of the bus is behind it.

grounding: It illustrates a boy with stomach aches before school who blames himself and hides the bullying from his parents for fear of making it worse.
